Regular Meetings are held on the 2nd Wednesday of every month at 6:00 p.m. Typically,
Adjourned Meetings are held on the last Friday of every month at 8:30 a.m.

In compliance with the American Disabilities Act, any person with a disability who

FROM:  Marcella Marlowe, Ph.D., City Manager
BY:  Stephanie Cao, City Attorney

DATE:  July 26, 2019
SUBJECT:  ORDINANCE TO CONSOLIDATE THE CITY’S REGULAR
  MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS WITH STATEWIDE PRIMARIES HELD
  IN NOVEMBER OF EVEN-NUMBERED YEARS (2nd READING)

STRATEGIC PLAN CRITICAL SUCCESS FACTORS

• Engaged and Connected Residents
• Efficient, Responsive, and Effective City Service
• Fiscally Responsible and Transparent City Government

BACKGROUND

On July 10, 2019, the City Council introduced Ordinance No. O-19-1353 to consolidate the
City’s regular municipal elections with statewide primaries held in November of even-numbered
years. Second reading of the Ordinance is required for adoption.

DISCUSSION

The Ordinance would change the General Municipal Election dates to align with the dates of
statewide elections in even years beginning in 2022, which will have the effect of extending two
terms of office to five years pursuant to Senate Bill 415. The Ordinance would amend Section
02.02.01 of the San Marino Municipal Code to include the new date of the City’s General
Municipal Election, changing the date of the City’s general municipal election from the first
Tuesday after the first Monday in November in odd-numbered years to the first Tuesday after
the first Monday in November in even-numbered years, effective in 2020, and extending City
Council terms in office accordingly.

  5
 FISCAL IMPACT & PROCUREMENT REVIEW

The estimated cost of the 2019 election is $103,000 – higher than normal due to a decreasing
number of cities conducting elections in odd years. Switching to even-numbered years could
result in more shared costs among cities and a decrease in cost for the City of San Marino in the
future.

LEGAL REVIEW

The City Attorney’s office has approved as to form.

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommends the City Council adopt Ordinance No. O-19-1353. If the City Council concurs
with staff’s recommendation, an appropriate motion would be:

“I move to adopt Ordinance No. O-19-1353.”

ATTACHMENTS

1. Ordinance No. O-19-1353
2. July 10, 2019 Staff Report re Ordinance No. O-19-1353

   ORDINANCE NO. O-19-1353

  AN ORDINANCE OF THE CITY OF SAN MARINO AMENDING
  SECTION 02.02.01 OF ARTICLE 2 OF CHAPTER 2 OF THE SAN
  MARINO MUNICIPAL CODE TO CHANGE THE DATE OF THE
  CITY’S GENERAL MUNICIPAL ELECTION FROM THE FIRST
  TUESDAY AFTER THE FIRST MONDAY IN NOVEMBER IN ODD-
  NUMBERED YEARS TO THE FIRST TUESDAY AFTER THE FIRST
  MONDAY IN NOVEMBER IN EVEN-NUMBERED YEARS,
  EFFECTIVE IN 2020, AND EXTENDING CITY COUNCIL TERMS IN
  OFFICE ACCORDINGLY

  WHEREAS, The City of San Marino is required under Senate Bill 415, which is
also known as the California Voter Participation Rights Act (Elections Code Sections
14050-14057), to change the date of the General Municipal Election to coincide with
statewide election dates no later than the November 8, 2022, statewide general election.

  WHEREAS, Prior to January 1, 2018, as required by SB 415, the San Marino
City Council previously adopted a plan to comply with Senate Bill 415 by consolidating
the General Municipal Election with the statewide general elections held in November of
even-numbered years beginning in 2022. This ordinance will implement the plan by the
date of the statewide election November 8, 2022, as required by SB 415.

  WHEREAS, by consolidating the General Municipal Election with the statewide
election held in November of even-numbered years, it is necessary to extend the terms
of incumbents by no more than 12 months as provided by Elections Code Section
10403.5(b). Subsequent terms of office shall remain the original four years, as provided
in the San Marino Municipal Code.

THE CITY COUNCIL OF THE CITY OF SAN MARINO DOES HEREBY ORDAIN AS
FOLLOWS:

Section 1.  Section 02.02.01 of Article 2 of Chapter 2 of the San Marino Municipal
Code regarding City elections is hereby amended to read as follows:

02.02.01: COUNCIL ELECTIONS:

Commencing in November, 2022, elections of members to the city council shall be held
on the first Tuesday after the first Monday in November of each even-numbered year,
rather than on the first Tuesday after the first Monday in November of each odd-
numbered year. The number of open positions on the council shall rotate between two
(2) positions in one election and three (3) positions in the subsequent election, pursuant
to the existing rotation in effect when this ordinance was adopted, unless a vacancy in
office occurs.

The current terms of members of the city council in office on the date this section takes
effect shall be extended accordingly. Those terms of office for those three (3) members
of the city council elected in November 2017, that would have been scheduled for

  7
 election in November 2021, are extended to be scheduled for election on the first
Tuesday after the first Monday in November 2022. Those terms of office for those two
(2) members of the city council to be elected in November 2019, are extended to be next
scheduled for election on the first Tuesday after the first Monday in November 2024. It
is the intent of the City Council that the term extensions adopted in this ordinance shall
apply only to the city council terms of office that commenced and will commence in 2017
and 2019, respectively, and that those terms shall be extended once for not more than
twelve (12) months each as defined in Elections Code 10403.5(b). All new city council
terms that commence after 2024 shall be for four (4) years.

Section 2.  As an ordinance relating to an election, this ordinance shall take effect
immediately upon adoption, and is operative following its approval by the Los Angeles
County Board of Supervisors. The City Clerk shall certify to the adoption of this
ordinance and transmit a certified copy of the ordinance to the Clerk of the Los Angeles
County Board of Supervisors with a request for approval forthwith, and shall give such
notice to the voters as is required by law. It is the intent of the City Council that this
change of election date shall be effective for the General Municipal Election that was
originally scheduled for the second Tuesday of November 2021. However, if for any
reason this ordinance is not approved by the Los Angeles County Board of Supervisors
by June 1, 2021, this ordinance shall have no further effect, and the General Municipal
Election shall be held on the second Tuesday in November of each odd numbered year
as currently specified in the San Marino Municipal Code.

FROM:  Marcella Marlowe, Ph.D., City Manager
BY:  Stephanie Cao, City Attorney and Carol Lynch, Senior Counsel

DATE:  July 10, 2019
SUBJECT:  APPROVAL OF ORDINANCE NO. O-19-1353 TO CONSOLIDATE
  THE CITY’S REGULAR MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS WITH
  STATEWIDE PRIMARIES HELD IN NOVEMBER OF EVEN-
  NUMBERED YEARS

STRATEGIC PLAN CRITICAL SUCCESS FACTORS

 Engaged and Connected Residents
 Efficient, Responsive, and Effective City Service
 Fiscally Responsible and Transparent City Government

BACKGROUND

Senate Bill 415 (SB 415) is known as the California Voter Participation Rights Act (Elections Code
Sections 14050-14057). In a bid to increase turnout rates for local elections, SB 415 amended
the California Elections Code pertaining to municipal election dates. The bill requires cities that
currently hold standalone municipal elections to eventually change their election dates to coincide
with statewide election dates, unless voter turnout rates for past standalone elections meet a
certain threshold. Like most cities, voter turnout in San Marino has not met that threshold.

DISCUSSION

The goal of SB 415 is to increase voter turnout rates for municipal elections, which tend to be
lower when elections are not held concurrently with statewide elections. For this purpose, a
statewide election is “an election held throughout the state” (Elections Code Sec. 357), which
now are only those elections held in March and November of even-numbered years.

In order to consolidate municipal and statewide elections, and thereby change the terms of office
for municipal officials, the City must adopt an ordinance pursuant to Elections Code Section
10000 et. seq.. If the City adopts an ordinance to consolidate elections, each municipal election
thereafter must be conducted on the date specified by the ordinance, unless the ordinance in

  11
 question is subsequently amended. However, at least one election must be held before the
ordinance can be amended again. (Elections Code Section 1301.)

In 2016, the City Council gave direction to change the General Municipal Election dates to align
with the dates of statewide elections in even years beginning in 2022, which will have the effect
of extending two terms of office to five years pursuant to SB 415. In order to implement the
City Council’s prior direction, it is necessary to amend Section 02.02.02 of the San Marino
Municipal Code to include the new date of the City’s General Municipal Election. The attached
ordinance makes that amendment.

FISCAL IMPACT & PROCUREMENT REVIEW

The estimated cost of the 2019 election is $103,000 – higher than normal due to a decreasing
number of cities conducting elections in odd years. Switching to even-numbered years could
result in more shared costs among cities and a decrease in cost for the City of San Marino in the
future.

LEGAL REVIEW

The City Attorney’s office has approved as to form.

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommends the City Council waive full reading and introduce for first reading by title only
Ordinance No. 0-19-1353. If the City Council concurs with staff’s recommendation, an
appropriate motion would be:

“I move to waive full reading and introduce for first reading by title only Ordinance No. 0-19-
1353, an Ordinance of the City Council of the City of San Marino amending section 02.02.02 of
Article 2 of Chapter 2 of the San Marino Municipal Code to change the date of the City’s general
municipal election from the first Tuesday after the first Monday in November in odd-numbered
years to the first Tuesday after the first Monday in November in even-numbered years, effective
in 2020, and extending City Council terms in office accordingly.”

ATTACHMENTS

1. Ordinance No. O-19-1353

 FROM:  Marcella Marlowe, Ph.D., City Manager
 BY:  Michael Throne, PE, Director of Parks and Public Works/City Engineer

 DATE:  July 26, 2019
 SUBJECT:  APPROVAL TO REFINE THE DECEMBER 2018 METRO MEASURE
  R SR-710 NORTH PROJECT PROPOSALS TO IMPROVE THE
  INTERSECTION  OF  HUNTINGTON  DRIVE/ATLANTIC
  BOULEVARD/GARFIELD AVENUE/LOS ROBLES AVENUE,
  SOLICIT FEEDBACK ON THE REFINEMENTS FROM THE PUBLIC
  SAFETY COMMISSION AND THE COMMUNITY, AND PRESENT
  REVISED PROPOSALS TO THE CITY COUNCIL IN SEPTEMBER

STRATEGIC PLAN CRITICAL SUCCESS FACTORS

• Engaged and Connected Residents
• Efficient, Responsive, and Effective City Services
• Safe Community
• Well-Maintained Infrastructure
• Fiscally Responsible and Transparent City Government

BACKGROUND

The City Council heard presentations related to the Metro Measure R 710 proposed projects on
Wednesday, July 10. Although much discussion occurred, many motions were offered, and three
were ultimately approved by a majority of the Council, the results left some confusion. In an
attempt to implement to the spirit of the decisions made by the City Council, and to receive
Council direction on any outstanding items, staff is returning for further discussion and
clarification related to the proposals.

DISCUSSION

On July 10, the Council considered seven motions in Council Member Jakubowski’s excused
absence. Four of those motions did not pass, as a result of a tie-vote.

  13
 The following three motions passed by a 3-1 vote:

  1. To direct the City Manager to communicate with Metro to withdraw a request for any
  funds relating to the syncing of traffic lights on Huntington Drive.
  2. To direct the City Manager to direct Metro that we are unwilling to accept any funds
  other than those to benefit the projects around our schools.
  3. To reject all funds on all intersections except for Atlantic.

The language in the motions are somewhat competing and contradictory. Nonetheless, we
believe that the City Council’s intention at that meeting was as follows:

  •  Project 1 (Intersection Improvements) – Reject the project and funding for three of the
  four intersections and reconsider the fourth intersection, Atlantic/Huntington/Los
  Robles/Garfield, at this July 26 meeting.
  •  Project 2 (Huntington Improvements) – Continue to reserve the Metro funding and direct
  staff to return to the City Council with refined and concrete proposals in September.
  •  Project 3 (Sierra Madre Improvements) – Reject all projects and funding associated with
  this item.
  •  Project 4 (Huntington Signal Synchronization) – Reject all projects and funding associated
  with this item.
  •  Project 5 (San Gabriel Signal Synchronization) – Reject all projects and funding associated
  with this item.

If the City Council agrees, the only remaining item for discussion is whether to direct the City
Manager to continue to reserve the Metro funding and further refine the
Atlantic/Huntington/Garfield/Los Robles intersection portion of Project Proposal #1.

FISCAL IMPACT & PROCUREMENT REVIEW

Metro reserved up to $32m of Measure R transportation sales tax funds for San Marino, attached
to five placeholder projects. Based on staff’s understanding of the City Council’s intentions on
July 10, the City will be reserving $6m pending refinements of Project 2 and rejecting $18m
related to Projects 3, 4, 5, and part of Project 1. A decision is pending today for the $8m
associated with the Atlantic/Huntington/Los Robles/Garfield intersection.

Funding rejected by San Marino will be reallocated to other local agencies in the San Gabriel
Valley that are pursuing traffic projects similar to those proposed for San Marino.

LEGAL REVIEW

The City Attorney has reviewed and approved the staff report as to legal form.

RECOMMENDATION
Based on the Public Safety Commission’s recommendation and staff’s professional expertise, we
recommend that the City Council direct the City Manager to work with the community and the
Public Safety Commission to refine the remaining projects from the December 2018 proposals.

  14
 If the City Council concurs with staff’s recommendation and staff’s summary of the Council’s July
10 intended actions, an appropriate motion would be:

“I move to vacate all motions approved at the July 10 City Council meeting related to this item
and direct the City Manager to take the following actions related to the five Metro Measure R
proposed projects:

  •  Project 1 (Intersection Improvements) – Continue to reserve the Metro funding of $8m
  for the Atlantic/Huntington/Los Robles/Garfield intersection, direct staff to return to the
  City Council with refined and concrete proposals in September for that intersection, and
  reject the remaining projects and $4m funding from this proposal.
  •  Project 2 (Huntington Improvements) – Continue to reserve the Metro funding of $6m
  and direct staff to return to the City Council with refined and concrete proposals in
  September.
  •  Project 3 (Sierra Madre Improvements) – Reject all projects and funding of $4m associated
  with this item.
  •  Project 4 (Huntington Signal Synchronization) – Reject all projects and funding of $7m
  associated with this item.
  •  Project 5 (San Gabriel Signal Synchronization) – Reject all projects and funding of $3m
  associated with this item.”

ATTACHMENTS

None.

FROM:  Marcella Marlowe, Ph.D., City Manager
BY:  John Incontro, Chief of Police

DATE:  July 26, 2019
SUBJECT:  2nd QUARTER POLICE DEPARTMENT REPORT

STRATEGIC PLAN CRITICAL SUCCESS FACTORS

• Engaged and Connected Residents
• Efficient, Responsive, and Effective City Services
• Safe Community
• Fiscally Responsible and Transparent City Government

BACKGROUND

On March 25, 2016, a Crime Reduction Plan was presented to the City Council outlining five
areas that would assist the Department’s effort to reduce crime. The Department’s last report
was May 8, 2019. Since that time Part 1 crimes have increased, including residential burglaries,
this year to date. The Department continues to work steadily to overcome the increase of all
Part 1 crimes.

As of the first quarter of 2019, the report has been refocused to provide the City Council an
overview of Department operations rather than a micro focus on crime. This change enables
the City Council to have a macro view of the Department.

DISCUSSION

The Department has lost ground in the reduction of crime this quarter. In May, the City
experienced 10 residential burglaries and, in June, five commercial burglaries. All other crimes
remained static throughout the quarter. These specific increases have resulted in an increase of
5% for all Part 1 crimes, or six crimes more this year compared to last year. The Department
has continued to spread the word on methods to reduce crime and how the residents can protect

  17
 their residences from burglaries. Similar increases are being felt throughout the San Gabriel
Valley and our partnership with other agencies has assisted us in solving these crimes.

The ongoing problem the Department faces with residential burglaries is the reluctance of
community members to install and use security systems. Of the 20 burglaries this year, 11 homes
did not have a security system and, of the remaining homes with security systems, three residents
did not have the system when they were victimized.

INVESTIGATIVE FOLLOW UP

Detectives are continuing their outstanding investigative work and detective-initiated arrests.
Five burglaries that occurred during this quarter have resulted in the identification of seven
suspects with arrest warrants and arrested six other suspects. Detectives have similar leads on
some of the other burglaries. The detectives have also made additional arrests related to financial
and traffic related crimes.

The primary reason for their success has been cooperation with different local task force
operations and other agencies within the Los Angeles region. The networking that our detectives
have utilized is having a positive impact on our crime reduction efforts.

COMMUNITY ENGAGEMENT

The Department hosted a Coffee with a Cop event that resulted in approximately 40 people
attending. This was the first co-hosted event with the Carver School Parent Teacher Association.
The event was successful with approximately 40 parents in attendance. We had four additional
events this quarter that, combined with the Coffee with a Cop, include over 90 residents.

The Department is now part of the Ring Law Enforcement Portal program. This portal allows
specific members of the Department to view video data from residents who voluntarily provide
the data from their doorbell camera device. It does not need to be a Ring device to provide the
video data, only a person connected to the Neighborhood App. The data that is provided could
be helpful in the identification and arrest of suspects involved in a crime.

Due to the end of school and summer vacations, our attempts to schedule neighborhood watch
meetings or other community events have been challenging. We have two events scheduled in
July and we are attempting to schedule additional events through the remainder of the summer.
The Department’s National Night Out event will be held on Tuesday, August 6, 2019, from 6-9
PM at the rear of the station.

  18
 PERSONNEL UPDATE

The Department has 30 authorized positions. As of July 16, 2019:
  • 26 full-time sworn positions are filled;
  • Two recruitment positions are filled; of our two recruitments, one is in training at the
  LASD Recruit Academy, and a second will begin academy training at Rio Hondo
  Community College in August; and
  • Two sworn officers are in the Field Training Program.

Additionally, we are processing four candidates for the two additional vacant positions. Of the
four, two have law enforcement experience and have completed a basic academy course.

FISCAL IMPACT & PROCUREMENT REVIEW

None.

LEGAL REVIEW

None.

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommends that the 2nd Quarter Police Department Report be discussed and if necessary,
provide direction to the Public Safety Commission to prioritize items for discussion. If Council
concurs, the appropriate action would be to receive and file.

 SUBJECT:  DISCUSSION REGARDING AN ORDINANCE OF THE CITY OF
  SAN MARINO AMENDING THE SAN MARINO MUNICIPAL
  CODE BY AMENDING THE REGULATIONS FOR FENCES AND
  WALLS IN RESIDENTIAL ZONES THAT ABUT ALLEYS

STRATEGIC PLAN CRITICAL SUCCESS FACTORS

  •  Beautiful, Preserved, Single-Family Residential Neighborhoods

BACKGROUND

The City Council has directed staff to draft an amendment to Chapter 23 Article 13,
Regulations for fences, walls and hedges in the R-1 Zone. The draft ordinance aims to only
consider amending the provisions related to walls or fences adjacent to an alley. The intent of
the draft ordinance is to allow for the ability to construct a new rear yard or side yard wall
adjacent to the property line and to allow for a height that maintains some level of privacy for
the residential property.

The current code requires that any wall adjacent to a street provide a setback of 18 inches
from the property line. In addition, the maximum height for the wall may not exceed 6 feet as
measured from the lowest grade. The original intent of the 18 inch setback was to provide
enough space between the property line and the wall to install landscaping. The landscaping in
front of the wall was intended to soften the appearance of the wall.

The proposed provision related to increased wall height is drafted to apply only when the grade
between the residential property and the alley is greater than 2 feet. This provision will ensure

  23
 that only those properties with this unique condition can benefit from this proposed code
amendment. In addition, due to the grade difference between the property and the alley,
language has been included to allow for walls to exceed the height limit of 6 feet and provide
privacy for that property. Staff also has added a requirement for the materials that can be used
to construct these walls, which requires that fences, walls, and gates shall be constructed of
solid wood, masonry, tubular steel, or wrought iron.

At the March 27 and April 24, 2019 Planning Commission meetings, a public hearing was
conducted, and staff presented the details surrounding the proposed ordinance. Several of the
Commissioners provided questions and comments regarding the Ordinance, which staff
addressed at both meetings. At the conclusion of the April meeting, the Planning Commission
approved the draft ordinance and recommended that the ordinance be presented to the City
Council through the formal public hearing process.

Typically, the standard procedure for introducing a code amendment is to provide public notice
and to introduce the ordinance to the Council for discussion and first reading. Due to the fact
that there has not been adequate discussion on the merits of this topic and the ordinance, staff
found that it would be appropriate to have a study session first before expending funds for the
notice and for the formal amendment process.

FISCAL IMPACT & PROCUREMENT REVIEW

None.

LEGAL REVIEW

The City Attorney has reviewed and approved the staff report as to legal form.

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommends the City Council discuss the merits of the proposed ordinance and direct
staff to proceed through the formal Code adoption process. If the Council concurs, an
appropriate motion would be:

“Motion to direct staff to proceed with the formal Code adoption process and return the
proposed ordinance to the City Council to conduct a public hearing for first reading of the
Ordinance.”

THE SAN MARINO CITY COUNCIL HEREBY ORDAINS AS FOLLOWS:

  Section 1.  Section 23.01.01 of Article 1 of Chapter 23 is hereby amended by adding
the following definition in alphabetical order.

  ALLEY: Any public roadway without curbs or sidewalks having a width that does not
exceed twenty (20) feet that is primarily used for access to the rear or side yards of abutting
residential properties.

  Section 2.  Subsections C and D of Section 23.13.04 of Article 13 of Chapter 23 of
the San Marino Municipal Code are hereby amended to read as follows:

C. Required Side Yard: All fences, gates, pilasters, yard walls and retaining walls located in the
required side yard shall conform to the requirements set forth herein:

1. Setback:

  a. No fence, pilaster, yard wall, or retaining wall shall be located less than two inches
  (2") from the side property line between two abutting residential properties, except
  by written mutual consent between the property owners.

  b. With the exception of fences, gates, pilasters, yard walls, or retaining walls abutting
  an alley, no fence, gate, pilaster, yard wall, or retaining wall in the required side yard
  facing a street on a corner lot shall be located less than eighteen inches (18") from the
  property line or the distance established by the DRC for safety reasons.

2. Height:

  a. Fences, yard walls, and retaining walls within the required side yard shall not exceed
  six feet (6') in height.

  b. Fences, gates, pilasters, yard walls, and retaining walls less than twenty feet (20') from
  the side street property line on a corner lot abutting a key lot shall not exceed four
  feet (4') in height.

  c. Fences, gates, pilasters, yard walls, and retaining walls less than twenty feet (20') from
  the front street property line abutting an alley shall not exceed four feet (4') in height.

  27
   d. Where the existing grade between a residential property that abuts an alley is greater
  than two feet (2’-0”), as measured from the residential property, the maximum height
  of the fence and wall may be increased to a total height of twelve feet (12’-0”).

3. Pilasters And Gates: No pilaster with cap, or gate facing the street, within the side yard of a
corner lot, shall exceed six inches (6") above the height of the applicable fence or yard wall limit
provided in subsection C2 of this section.

4. Ornamental Features: Ornamental features or lights on gate pilasters shall not exceed twelve
inches (12") above the height of the pilaster, or the height determined by the Design Review
Committee.

5. Finished Material:

  a. Fences, walls, and gates located adjacent to an alley shall be constructed of solid wood,
  masonry, tubular steel, or wrought iron.

D. Required Rear Yard: All fences, gates, pilasters, yard walls and retaining walls located in the
required rear yard shall conform to the requirements contained herein:

1. Setback:

  a. No fence, yard wall or retaining wall between two abutting residential properties shall
  be located less than two inches (2") from the rear property line, except by written mutual
  consent between the property owners.

  b. With the exception of fences, gates, pilasters, yard walls or retaining walls abutting an
  alley, no fences, gates, pilasters, yard walls or retaining walls shall be located less than
  eighteen inches (18") from the rear property line facing the street of a lot.

2. Height:

  a. Fences, yard walls and retaining walls within the required rear yard shall not exceed
  six feet (6') in height, provided:

  b. Fences, gates, pilasters, yard walls and retaining walls less than twenty feet (20') from
  the side street property line on a corner lot abutting a key lot shall not exceed four
  feet (4') in height.

  c. Where the existing grade between a residential property that abuts an alley is greater
  than two feet (2’-0”), as measured from the residential property, the maximum height
  of the fence and wall may be increased to a total height of twelve feet (12’-0”).

3. Pilasters And Gates: No pilaster with cap, or gate facing the street, within the rear yard of a
corner lot, shall exceed six inches (6") above the height of the applicable fence or yard wall limit
provided in subsection D2 of this Section.
